theme: Sabbath disputes; the Twelve; the Sermon on the Plain
readingInstruction: Read Luke 6:1-49. Sabbath disputes, the choosing of the Twelve after a night of prayer, and the Sermon on the Plain. Compare it with the Sermon on the Mount from Matthew 5 to 7.
settingTheScene: Opposition from the religious leaders grows over the Sabbath. Then Jesus spends a night in prayer on the mountain, chooses twelve apostles, and comes down to a level place to teach a great crowd. The Sermon on the Plain is shorter than Matthew’s version and focused on a few things: blessings and woes, love for enemies, mercy, and obedience. It is likely the same teaching given on another occasion, or a summary.
observation: “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” (6:5).
“In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God” (6:12).
“Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (6:20).
“But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation” (6:24).
“But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you” (6:27).
“Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” (6:36).
“Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and not do what I tell you?” (6:46).
“But the one who hears and does not do is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation” (6:49).
interpretation:
The Sabbath conflicts show what is at stake. The disciples pluck grain, and Jesus defends them, citing David, and declares himself lord of the Sabbath. On another Sabbath, he heals a man’s withered hand, and asks, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?” The Pharisees are filled with fury.

Then comes the night of prayer. Before choosing the Twelve, Jesus spends the whole night in prayer. A major decision is preceded by deep communion with the Father. He names twelve, including Judas Iscariot, “who became a traitor.” The Twelve are the foundation of the renewed Israel.

On the plain, with a great crowd, he gives the Beatitudes with a difference. Luke records four blessings and four woes. “Blessed are you who are poor… hungry… weep… hated.” And “woe to you who are rich… full… laugh… spoken well of.” These are not general wishes. Jesus speaks to his disciples, and he puts the reversal clearly: those who look secure now may be empty later, and those who suffer for him will be rewarded.

The heart of the sermon is love for enemies. “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.” This is not just a rule for sentiment but for action: give, lend, and expect nothing back. The standard is the character of God himself: “Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.” The Father is kind even to the ungrateful and the evil.

Then come warnings about judging, the log in the eye, and a tree known by its fruit. The sermon ends with the two builders. The one who hears and does is like the one who dug deep and laid the foundation on rock. The difference is obedience, and the question is pointed: “Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and not do what I tell you?”
connection: Matthew 5 to 7 is the longer Sermon on the Mount, and you read it in Unit 15. Psalm 1 is the background to the two ways. 1 Samuel 21:1-6 is the story of David’s eating the bread. Romans 12:14-21 repeats Jesus’ teaching on enemies. 1 Peter 2:21-23 says Christ left us an example. James 1:22 says to be doers of the word. Ephesians 4:32 says to forgive as God in Christ forgave you.
application:
Pray through the night, or at least for an hour, before a significant decision.

Choose one enemy or difficult person and do something good for them this week, without expecting anything back.

Ask the Lord’s own question of yourself: do I call him Lord and do what he says?
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being Lord of the Sabbath.
Thank him for praying all night before choosing his apostles.
Ask him to help you do what he says, not only hear.
